newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Second Albanian vote seals Socialist landslide.
newsitem.headline: Second Albanian vote seals Socialist landslide.

text.p: Albanians voting for a second consecutive Sunday sealed a landslide victory for the opposition Socialist party in an election intended to end months of violence in which over 1,500 people have died.

The Socialists had already won more than 80 of 155 assembly seats in the first round last week and run-off votes in 34 districts where no candidate had won 50 percent will merely determine the size of their majority.
Officials said up to three constituencies would go through to yet another round of voting next Sunday.

The election was called in March after the collapse of popular pyramid savings funds triggered an uprising that forced President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party government to resign after five years in power.
Socialist leader Fatos Nano said on Sunday he would be the next prime minister while the president has said he will resign once a left-of-centre government takes office.
Around 500,000 of Albania's 3.4 million people were eligible to vote on Sunday, but the Socialist win reduced interest and turnout was low. It was unclear when the results would be announced.
"The turnout today was lower than in the first round...20 percent less in Tirana," Thimio Kondi, secretary of the Central Electoral Commission, told Albanian television.
Scorching temperatures of 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) also dampened voter enthusiasm.
"People are indifferent now. They are tired of it all," said Nazmi Kucu, chairman of a poll booth in central Tirana.
Kondi said further voting would be required next Sunday in seats where results are in dispute.
"There will be one constituency, maybe two, three at the most, that will be involved in a further round of voting next Sunday," Kondi said.

The first round of voting was declared "adequate and acceptable" by the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) that, together with the Council of Europe, had about 450 observers monitoring the Balkan nation's election.

A 7,000-strong International Protection Force sent to Albania in April has also helped to guard polling stations to ensure Albania's fourth multi-party election since the 1990 fall of communism ran smoothly.
Catherine Lalumiere, who is to produce an OSCE report on monitoring the vote, said she had seen no major irregularities.
She was aware both the Democrats and Socialists had complained of intimidation and procedural violations.

"I have noted that certain people have drawn attention to problems," she told reporters. "It is my impression that those people stressing this are trying to undermine the credibility of the election as a whole. In whose interest is it to do so?"
Lalumiere said she hoped to publish a final report on the election within a week.

Polling stations on Sunday opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 6 p.m., three hours earlier than originally stated in the election law to guard against cheating and ensure the safety of voters and monitors. A 10 p.m to 5 a.m. curfew is still in effect under a state of emergency introduced in March.

The OSCE and Kondi said police were called to deal with incidents of armed people at polling booths at Kavaje, 50 km (30 miles) southwest of Tirana, Kruje just outside Tirana and Shkoder in the country's north. There were no shots fired.

The runoff ballots will determine whether the Socialists, along with two allied parties, will gain the two-thirds majority to enable them to push important legislation through parliament -- and vote in a new head of state.
